samples.summary: Cross-provider email merge is switched on with no cleanup of User rows already created from unverified GitHub emails
samples.evidence:
This PR makes the email address the shared identity across two providers: `googleAuthCallback` (auth.controller.ts:280) calls the same `findOrCreateUser`, which matches on `email` alone (`prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: data.email } })`, user.service.ts:41-45). The PR's own rationale (github.strategy.ts:43-47, docs/design/backend.md risk entry) states that before this change GitHub's primary address was taken without reading its `verified` flag, and that an unverified address can be the primary. So rows keyed on an address the holder never proved ownership of may already exist in any deployment.

Attack: Mallory signed in with GitHub at any point before this change while `victim@corp.com` sat as her primary, unverified address — auth.controller.ts (pre-change `email: emails?.[0]?.value`) created a User row keyed on it and gave her a session. After this PR ships, the real owner of `victim@corp.com` clicks "Continue with Google"; `GoogleStrategy.validate` correctly confirms Google verified the address, and `findOrCreateUser` then resolves it to Mallory's *existing* row rather than creating one. The victim and Mallory are now the same user: Mallory's outstanding access/refresh cookies (7-day refresh, auth.controller.ts:46) authenticate as the victim and see every workspace, document and datasource the victim creates.

The forward path is closed (`verifiedEmail` at github.strategy.ts:57-64 now refuses), but nothing addresses the backfill: there is no `emailVerified` column on `User` (prisma/schema.prisma), and no migration in this change or any prior one touches the users table for this (I listed all 23 files under packages/backend/prisma/migrations/). There is therefore no way for an operator to tell which existing rows are safe to merge into, and no re-verification step on first cross-provider sign-in.
searchedFor: Glob packages/backend/prisma/migrations/*/migration.sql (all 23 enumerated; none touch User email verification)
Grep 'email' across packages/backend/src (17 files; no email-verification column, no re-confirmation flow, no invite-by-email path)
Read packages/backend/src/user/user.service.ts findOrCreateUser
Grep 'emailVerified|verified' in prisma/schema.prisma region for User
Read docs/design/backend.md and docs/tasks/active/20260915-google-oauth-login-todo.md for any stated migration/backfill plan

samples.summary: An `http://` GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL now silently strips `Secure` and `__Host-` from the session, refresh and state cookies on a production install that sets no GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL
samples.evidence:
`isSecureCookie()` used to read only `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` and fall through to `NODE_ENV === 'production'`. The new loop at oauth-state.ts:244-248 returns `false` as soon as *either* variable starts with `http://`, and `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` is documented as optional (backend README env table: Required = No, GitHub falls back to the URL registered on the OAuth app; github-auth.guard.ts:66-76 relies on exactly that configuration existing).

Concrete downgrade: a deployment running with `NODE_ENV=production`, no `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`, currently gets `isSecureCookie() === true` from the NODE_ENV fallback — `Secure` cookies named `__Host-wafflebase_session` / `__Host-wafflebase_refresh` / `__Host-wafflebase_oauth_state`. The operator then enables Google and pastes the value this PR's own README hunk shows as the example, `GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL=http://localhost:3000/auth/google/callback` (packages/backend/README.md, GOOGLE_* block). The loop hits `http://` on the second name and returns `false`. Every login cookie is now issued without `Secure` and without the prefix.

That is precisely the property oauth-state.ts:24-47 and :66-84 describe as the *only* defence against a sibling-subdomain foothold setting `wafflebase_session=<attacker JWT>; Domain=<parent>` (session fixation) or planting the browser's half of the double-submit `state`. It also silently flips `cliLoginAvailable()` (github-auth.guard.ts:79) to false. Nothing fails loudly — the only signal is the once-per-process warning at github-auth.guard.ts:267, which a running deployment will not re-emit until the next restart's first login.

Grep 'useSecureCookies|isSecureCookie' across packages/backend/src
Read packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts (cliLoginAvailable, insecureProductionOrigin, loopbackCallback — the latter two still read only GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL)
Read the README GOOGLE_* / COOKIE_SECURE hunks in the diff

samples.summary: The browser OAuth `state` cookie is one provider-agnostic namespace, so a state minted by /auth/google satisfies /auth/github/callback and vice versa
samples.evidence:
`startWebOAuthLogin` writes a single cookie, `oauthStateCookieName()` (web-oauth-login.ts:44), for both providers, and `consumeWebOAuthState` (web-oauth-login.ts:68-74) reads that same name from both callbacks — auth.controller.ts:164 (GitHub) and auth.controller.ts:268 (Google). `webOAuthStateMatches` (oauth-state.ts:177-185) compares only `WEB_STATE_PREFIX + sha256(cookieSecret)`; nothing in the state or the cookie records which authorization server it was minted for.

So the double-submit pair is a bearer token for *either* callback. If an attacker learns an in-flight `state` value — it travels in the `Location:` header to the provider, in the provider's access logs, in browser history on a shared machine, and in any intercepting proxy — they can, within the 10-minute cookie lifetime, hand the victim `\/auth/github/callback?code=<code the attacker minted against their own GitHub account>&state=<leaked state>`. The victim's cookie still matches, `finishWebLogin` runs, and the victim's browser is issued a session for the attacker's account (session fixation / cross-provider mix-up). Binding the cookie name or the state payload to the provider would make the leaked half useless on the other route.

I could not complete the chain to a leak the attacker controls unaided — CORS is pinned to FRONTEND_URL (main.ts:73-78), so the 302's Location cannot be read cross-origin — hence low confidence. The state-reuse property itself is directly readable in the two call sites above.
searchedFor: Read packages/backend/src/auth/web-oauth-login.ts and oauth-state.ts (single OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE_BASE, no provider field in WebOAuthState)
Grep 'consumeWebOAuthState|startWebOAuthLogin' across packages/backend/src (only the two guards and the two callbacks)
Read packages/backend/src/main.ts CORS configuration

samples.summary: The GitHub callback still creates a User row and a Workspace before checking `state`; only the new Google callback was fixed
samples.evidence:
`googleAuthCallback` deliberately orders the check first and says so (auth.controller.ts:262-271: "Checked *before* the user is upserted, so a refused callback leaves no row (and no workspace) behind"). `githubAuthCallback` still calls `this.userService.findOrCreateUser(...)` at auth.controller.ts:126-131, and only then reaches the `state` validation at :155-166.

An unauthenticated attacker can walk GitHub's authorize endpoint against this deployment's public `client_id` with their own GitHub account, take the resulting `code`, and POST/GET it to `/auth/github/callback` with no `state` at all. `AuthGuard('github')` exchanges it and `validate` succeeds, so `findOrCreateUser` runs: a `User` row, a `Workspace` and a `WorkspaceMember` are committed (user.service.ts:50-64) for a sign-in that is then refused and redirected to `?error=oauth_state`. Repeatable at the route's 10/min/IP throttle, from as many GitHub accounts and IPs as the attacker has, and the rows are indistinguishable from real signups. Pre-existing, but this change makes the asymmetry explicit by fixing only one of the two callbacks.
searchedFor: Read packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts githubAuthCallback vs googleAuthCallback ordering
Read packages/backend/src/user/user.service.ts findOrCreateUser side effects

samples.summary: Attacker-chosen Google `displayName` reaches an unguarded unique workspace slug, where a collision aborts signup after the User row is already committed
samples.evidence:
`GoogleStrategy.validate` sets `username: usernameFor(profile, email)` = `profile.displayName?.trim()` (google.strategy.ts:74-76, :128), which is a free-form, user-editable string on a Google account. `findOrCreateUser` slugs it directly — `newUser.username.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g,'-')... + '-s-workspace'` — and calls `prisma.workspace.create({ data: { name, slug } })` (user.service.ts:54-61) without the collision handling that `WorkspaceService.generateUniqueSlug` provides (workspace.service.ts:22, :277-281). `Workspace.slug` is `@unique` (prisma/schema.prisma:168) and the three writes are not wrapped in a transaction.

Before this change the only source of `username` was a GitHub login name, which is globally unique and restricted to `[A-Za-z0-9-]`, so the derived slug effectively could not collide. A Google `displayName` can be set to anything, so an attacker can pre-create `john-smith-s-workspace` and every subsequent "John Smith" Google signup throws P2002 *after* the `User` row is committed — the victim ends up with a user row, no workspace and no membership, and retrying just re-finds the broken row by email. Denial of signup plus a persistent half-created account, from an unauthenticated route.

Grep 'slug' in packages/backend/prisma/schema.prisma (Workspace.slug @unique)
Grep 'slug' in packages/backend/src/workspace (generateUniqueSlug exists but is not used by findOrCreateUser)

samples.summary: Google `email_verified` is trusted alone for the cross-provider merge, with no `hd` / hosted-domain restriction and no linking confirmation
samples.evidence:
`resolveEmail` returns `verified: true` on `email_verified` / `verified_email` alone (google.strategy.ts:58-63), and the controller then merges on that address into any pre-existing row (auth.controller.ts:280-285). Google sets `email_verified: true` for every Google Workspace account in a domain, including domains an administrator acquired after the original organisation let them lapse — the well-known "Sign in with Google" domain-takeover caveat. Because the merge is unconditional and silent, whoever later controls a Workspace domain can mint an account at any address in it and sign straight into the existing Wafflebase user keyed on that address, with no prompt, no notification, and no record on the `User` row that a second provider was ever attached (`authProvider` is stamped once at creation — docs/design/backend.md).

The usual mitigations are absent: no `hd` claim check, no allowlist of merge-eligible domains, no "this email already has an account created with GitHub — confirm linking" step, and no notification on first cross-provider sign-in. Surfaced because the merge is what this change introduces; the docs record it as an accepted decision rather than a mitigated one.

Grep 'hd|hosted_domain|hostedDomain' across packages/backend/src (no matches)
Grep 'email' across packages/backend/src for any linking-confirmation or notification path
Read docs/design/backend.md 'Provider identity is the email address' risk entry

samples.summary: The Google callback performs the full token exchange and userinfo fetch before any `state` check, so an unauthenticated caller can drive outbound requests
samples.evidence: `GoogleCallbackGuard` (auth.controller.ts:252) runs `AuthGuard('google')`, which exchanges `?code=` at Google's token endpoint and fetches userinfo, before the controller body's `state` check at :265-271 ever runs. Same shape as the GitHub callback. Bounded by the 10/min/IP `@Throttle` and pointed at fixed provider endpoints, so it is not SSRF — but a callback that will be refused anyway costs two outbound round trips first. Checking `isWebOAuthState(req.query.state)` inside the guard, ahead of `super.canActivate`, would short-circuit it.

verdict.reason: No counterexample exists in this repository. `findOrCreateUser` (packages/backend/src/user/user.service.ts:40-48) resolves an account by `email` alone and returns any pre-existing row irrespective of `authProvider`; the Google callback calls it directly and immediately mints session/refresh cookies (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:280-291 -> finishWebLogin:303-317), with no provider reconciliation or re-verification step on a first cross-provider sign-in. The `User` model carries no verification state (packages/backend/prisma/schema.prisma:1-21), and no migration or data-migration script addresses existing rows: the only non-SQL migration artifact is the unrelated workspace backfill (packages/backend/prisma/migrations/data-migration-workspaces.ts), and the users table is untouched since the initial schema (packages/backend/prisma/migrations/20250830053514_initial_schema/migration.sql:2,23). Docs acknowledge that GitHub's primary address was previously taken without reading its `verified` flag and that an unverified address can be primary (docs/design/backend.md:893-908; packages/backend/src/auth/github.strategy.ts:36-56), yet neither the design doc, the task todo/lessons files, nor packages/backend/README.md:44-54 contain any backfill, audit or operator-action guidance. The forward guards (github.strategy.ts:57-64,132-137; google.strategy.ts:118-123) close new sign-ins only. The residual vector is in-lane for Security (authentication/account-merge leading to takeover): a row created earlier from an unverified GitHub primary equal to a victim's address becomes the account the verified Google owner is merged into, and the earlier holder's outstanding 7-day refresh cookie (auth.controller.ts:46,462-468) then authenticates as that user.

verdict.reason: The code is exactly as described. oauth-state.ts:244-248 iterates ['GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL','GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL'] and returns false on the first value starting with 'http://', so the NODE_ENV=production fallback at line 249 is never reached when GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL is unset and GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL is http. That configuration is explicitly supported: github-auth.guard.ts:66-76 and README.md:184-198 both state an install with no GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL under NODE_ENV=production currently gets useSecureCookies()===true, and README.md:46-47 hands the operator the http://localhost:3000/auth/google/callback example. The flip propagates to secure: at oauth-state.ts:141 and :190 and to hostPrefixedCookieName() at :62-64, dropping Secure and the __Host- prefix from wafflebase_session / _refresh / _oauth_state / _cli_state — the property lines 22-47 and 66-84 describe as the sole defence against sibling-subdomain cookie tossing and session fixation — and also flips cliLoginAvailable() (github-auth.guard.ts:78-79). No guard prevents it: COOKIE_SECURE=true (line 241) is an operator opt-in, and insecureProductionOrigin() (github-auth.guard.ts:92-98) only emits a log and is itself derived from useSecureCookies(). oauth-state.spec.ts:162-181 codifies the new precedence rather than guarding against the downgrade. In-lane for the security rubric (auth/crypto cookie protections, sensitive data exposure); trigger needs an operator misconfiguration, which fits major rather than critical, but it is real and reachable.

finding.summary: Cross-provider account takeover: the GitHub side has no verified-email check, and this change makes email the shared identity across two providers
finding.evidence: This change makes `findOrCreateUser` (packages/backend/src/user/user.service.ts:41, matches on `email` alone) the merge point for two providers. `GoogleStrategy.validate` carefully refuses an unverified address (google.strategy.ts:81), and the diff's own docs assert the GitHub side needs no equivalent because "on the `user:email` scope it returns only addresses it has verified" (google.strategy.ts:19-20, docs/design/backend.md:896-903). Nothing in this repo enforces that: `GitHubStrategy.validate` takes `emails?.[0]?.value` (github.strategy.ts:77) with no `verified` filter, and GitHub's `/user/emails` returns *unverified* addresses too (each entry carries a `verified` flag that is never read here). `github.strategy.spec.ts` only asserts endpoint URLs, never verification. Attack: attacker adds the victim's Google address to their own GitHub account (unverified — they cannot verify it), signs in via `GET /auth/github`, and if that address lands at `emails[0]` the callback calls `findOrCreateUser({email: victim@…})` (auth.controller.ts:126) and issues a session for the victim's Google-created Wafflebase account. Before this change the same weakness only merged GitHub↔GitHub; this change extends the blast radius to every Google-created account and simultaneously documents the assumption as safe. The mitigation the Google side has (`verified === true`) is absent on the GitHub side.

verdict.reason: The finding claims GitHubStrategy has no verified-email check, citing `emails?.[0]?.value` at github.strategy.ts:77. That is not what the repository contains. `verifiedEmail()` (github.strategy.ts:57-64) filters profile emails to those whose `verified` flag is set via `isFlagSet` (line 60), picking the verified primary or any other verified address (line 62); the strategy passes `allRawEmails: true` (line 102) specifically so the `verified`/`primary` flags are not stripped by passport-github2; and `validate()` (lines 124-137) throws `UnauthorizedException('GitHub account has no verified email address...')` when no verified address exists, exactly mirroring the Google side (google.strategy.ts:118-123). The spec also covers it: github.strategy.spec.ts:129-171 asserts `_allRawEmails`, primary-verified selection, fallback when the primary is unverified, and rejection of profiles with nothing verified or explicitly unverified. GitHubStrategy is the only GitHub profile-to-user path (only other references are auth.module.ts and github-auth.guard.ts), so the email merge point into findOrCreateUser is guarded on both provider sides. The alleged mitigation is present, so the cross-provider takeover vector described does not exist.

finding.summary: `isSecureCookie()` still reads only `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`; a deployment that states its https scheme via the new required `GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL` gets non-`Secure`, non-`__Host-` session and state cookies
finding.evidence: `isSecureCookie()` (oauth-state.ts:229-240) decides `Secure` and the `__Host-` prefix for the session, refresh, oauth-state, cli-state and login-return cookies from `COOKIE_SECURE`, then `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`, then `NODE_ENV`. This change introduces `GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL`, which `oauth-providers.ts:21` makes *mandatory* for Google and which states the deployment's public scheme just as GitHub's does — but it is never consulted. `github-auth.guard.ts:66-72` documents that an install with **no** `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` is a supported working deployment (GitHub falls back to the URL registered on the OAuth app). So an https install that sets `GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL=https://app.example.com/auth/google/callback`, omits `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`, and does not set `NODE_ENV=production` falls through to line 239 and issues every login cookie without `Secure` and without the `__Host-` prefix. That is exactly the write-restriction the module says is the only thing stopping sibling-subdomain cookie tossing of the double-submit secret and of `wafflebase_session` (oauth-state.ts:26-47, 66-84) — i.e. session fixation. Adding a second callback URL without teaching `isSecureCookie()` about it leaves a configuration that looks fully specified but silently downgrades the cookies.

verdict.reason: The finding's central factual claim — that `isSecureCookie()` "still reads only GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL" and that `GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL` "is never consulted" — is not true of this repository. oauth-state.ts:244 loops over `['GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL', 'GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL']`, testing each for an `https://`/`http://` prefix before the `NODE_ENV` fallback at :249. In the precise deployment the finding describes (https GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL, no GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL, NODE_ENV not production), the GitHub entry is an empty string matching neither prefix, the loop continues, and Google's https prefix returns true — so the session/refresh/oauth-state/cli-state/login-return cookies do get `Secure` and the `__Host-` prefix. oauth-state.spec.ts:162-170 asserts exactly this case, including `sessionCookieName()` === `__Host-wafflebase_session`, and the doc comment at :214-222 describes the two-variable rule. Grep confirms oauth-state.ts:239 is the only definition of the predicate and :260 the only exported wrapper used by auth.controller.ts:492, cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:62, login-return-path.ts:95 and github-auth.guard.ts:79,95, so no stale copy exhibits the claimed behaviour. The finding's cited range (229-240) is the tail of the doc comment, not the decision logic. The only remaining GitHub-first asymmetry (http GitHub URL beating an https Google URL) is a documented precedence for a self-contradictory config and is not the scenario claimed.
